title: Bees on the Rooftop
context:
A. Rooftop hives have multiplied in many cities over the past two decades. In London, the number of registered colonies rose from fewer than 1,000 in 2008 to well over 5,000 ten years later, and comparable increases have been recorded in Paris, New York and Tokyo. Enthusiasts often argue that a city is a kinder home for bees than farmland, partly because gardens and parks flower over a long season and partly because far fewer agricultural pesticides are sprayed there. Yet a growing number of ecologists are asking whether this boom is as harmless as it looks.

B. A study carried out in a group of public parks found that wherever honeybee numbers were highest, wild bumblebees and solitary bees made noticeably fewer visits to flowers. Honeybees can strip a blossom of nectar very quickly, leaving little for other insects, and many native species forage only a few hundred metres from their nests, so they cannot simply move elsewhere. The researchers pointed out that the supply of flowers in any city is finite. Adding hives without adding plants, they warned, may merely shift food from one group of pollinators to another.

C. Urban honey has become a subject of scientific curiosity as well as a popular gift. Laboratory tests on samples from several cities have detected traces of lead and cadmium, but always at levels well below the limits set for food safety. Pollen grains in a jar can also be counted under a microscope, which reveals which plants the bees visited and therefore something of the neighbourhood's vegetation. Keepers report that honey from one district can taste markedly different from honey produced only two kilometres away, a variation that supermarket blends deliberately avoid.

D. Many newcomers to the hobby lose their first colony within a year, and the cause is rarely the cold. More often the bees starve in late winter after the keeper has taken too much honey, or they are weakened by parasitic mites that went unnoticed. Beekeeping associations therefore run courses for beginners and pair them with experienced mentors who visit the hives in person. In some countries, owners are legally required to register their colonies, which allows inspectors to trace outbreaks of disease quickly and advise nearby keepers.

E. Relations with neighbours can be delicate. Surveys show that many people fear being stung, and the sight of a swarm hanging from a tree can cause alarm even though swarming bees are usually docile. Some keepers therefore place a tall fence or hedge in front of the hive entrance, forcing the bees to climb steeply and fly above head height, away from pedestrians. A number of local councils have gone further and limit how many hives a single property may hold, depending on its size. Open communication, many keepers say, prevents most disputes.

F. Conservation groups increasingly suggest that people who want to help pollinators should look beyond the honeybee. They recommend sowing wildflower strips, leaving corners of gardens untidy, and installing small wooden boxes with drilled tubes where solitary bees can nest. Some critics also doubt the motives behind hives installed on the roofs of banks and hotels, arguing that these are mainly a form of advertising which says little about genuine environmental commitment. A few companies have responded by spending their budgets on planting schemes instead of on insects.

title: Power from the Tides
context:
A. Tides are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the moon, with a smaller contribution from the sun, and in most coastal regions the sea rises and falls twice a day. This regularity gives tidal power a quality that few renewable sources can claim. Wind farms and solar panels depend on weather that can change within hours, whereas the timing and size of tides can be calculated for decades ahead with great accuracy. Engineers therefore regard tidal electricity as a dependable partner for more variable sources, even if it is unlikely ever to supply a whole nation on its own.

B. The oldest large tidal station still operating is on the Rance estuary in northern France, which opened in 1966. It works by trapping water behind a barrage, a wall built across the river mouth, and releasing it through turbines. The plant has produced electricity for more than fifty years, but its construction altered the estuary dramatically. Sand and mud now settle in different places, mudflats that once fed wading birds have changed, and fish migration has been disrupted. Such effects have made later proposals for barrages far more controversial than the French example once was.

C. A newer approach avoids walls altogether. Submerged turbines, resembling small wind turbines, are fixed to the seabed in channels where currents run fast. A pioneering array in the north of Scotland has fed power to the national grid since 2018. Because the blades turn slowly, usually only a few times a minute, studies using underwater cameras suggest that seals and fish tend to swim around them rather than being struck. Developers argue that this makes the technology gentler on wildlife than a barrage, although long-term monitoring is still in its early stages.

D. Money remains the biggest obstacle. Each unit of electricity from a tidal turbine currently costs several times more than the same amount from offshore wind. Equipment must survive in water that corrodes metal and constantly pushes against moving parts, so maintenance is demanding. Repair crews can only reach the machines during short periods of calm weather between tides, and a single failed bearing may take weeks to replace. These difficulties make private investors cautious, since they cannot be sure that the machines will last as long as the loans that paid for them.

E. Geography limits where tidal schemes can succeed. A difference of at least five metres between high and low water is generally needed to make a project worthwhile, and only a small share of the world's coastline meets that standard. The Bay of Fundy in Canada, the Severn Estuary in Britain and parts of the Korean peninsula are among the exceptional places. Even in these locations, the best sites are sometimes far from cities, so new power lines must be built to carry the electricity to the people who need it.

F. Researchers are exploring several ways to improve the economics. One idea is the tidal lagoon, an artificial ring of sea wall that encloses a shallow area and so affects a smaller stretch of coast than a river barrage. Another is to moor turbines beneath floating platforms that can be towed to shore for repair. Governments can also help by guaranteeing a fixed price for the electricity for many years, and some island communities have given residents a share of the income, which has increased local support for projects.

title: Why Teenagers Stay Up Late
context:
A. Parents often accuse teenagers of laziness, but biology offers a kinder explanation. During adolescence the body clock shifts, and the brain begins releasing melatonin, the hormone that prepares us for sleep, roughly two hours later than it does in childhood. As a result, many fifteen-year-olds do not feel drowsy until around eleven at night, however early they go to bed. Scientists stress that this is a normal developmental change rather than a flaw of character, and that it fades again in the early twenties.

B. Electronic devices are frequently blamed for late nights. In one national survey, about seven in ten teenagers admitted to using a phone while lying in bed. The blue light given off by screens is thought to delay melatonin release further, but some sleep researchers believe its role has been overstated. They argue that a thrilling video, a heated group chat or the fear of missing something online keeps the mind alert, so what teenagers watch may matter as much as the light itself.

C. Several school districts have experimented with later mornings. In one American county, the first bell was moved from 7.30 to 8.40, and researchers followed the students for two years. On average, they slept 45 minutes longer on school nights. Attendance rose, fewer pupils fell asleep in lessons, and examination results improved modestly. Critics had predicted that teenagers would simply stay up later, but the data showed that bedtimes barely changed, so the extra time in the morning became extra sleep.

D. The consequences of chronic sleep loss extend well beyond yawning in class. Teenagers who regularly sleep fewer than seven hours are more likely to report anxiety and low mood. Memory is also affected, because the brain strengthens newly learned material during deep sleep, and a shortened night leaves less time for that process. Among drivers aged seventeen to nineteen, drowsiness is a recognised factor in road accidents, particularly in the early hours of the morning and late in the afternoon.

E. Many adolescents try to repay their sleep debt at weekends. Sleeping until noon on Saturday and Sunday, however, pushes the body clock later still, so that getting up on Monday feels like flying across several time zones. Researchers call this mismatch between the school-week and weekend rhythms 'social jet lag'. Although a long lie-in brings temporary relief, studies suggest it does not fully repair the damage caused by a week of short nights, and the benefits for attention and mood are only partial.

F. Doctors suggest a few practical habits. Keeping the same bedtime and wake-up time every day helps to steady the body clock, and opening the curtains to bright daylight soon after waking helps to anchor it. Drinks containing caffeine are best avoided after midday, since the stimulant can linger in the body for many hours. Yet schools that wish to start later often meet resistance, because sports fixtures and bus timetables are arranged around the existing day and would be costly to change.

title: Keeping Small Languages Alive
context:
A. Linguists estimate that around half of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken today may disappear before the end of this century, which means that, on average, one falls silent every few weeks. Violent suppression is now a less common cause than economic calculation. Parents who live in minority communities frequently decide that their children will have better chances of finding jobs and doing well at school if they learn a dominant national or international language, and so they stop speaking the older one at home. Within a single generation, a thriving tongue can become one that only grandparents remember.

B. One of the most successful responses has been the language nest, a pre-school in which elderly fluent speakers spend the whole day talking to very young children exclusively in the heritage language. The first nests were set up by community volunteers in the 1980s, without waiting for official support, and they spread rapidly because families could see the results. By the time the children reach primary school they can understand their elders and manage in two languages, something classroom lessons for older learners rarely achieve.

C. Documentation offers a different kind of protection. Linguists record the voices of the last remaining speakers, compile dictionaries and write down traditional stories, creating archives that may be useful for centuries. Many specialists, however, warn that a recording is not the same as a living language: a language that exists only on a hard drive cannot be used to joke, argue or tell a child to come home. Ethical questions also arise. In some communities, certain words may be spoken only during ceremonies, and elders insist that the community, not the researcher, must decide who can listen to the recordings.

D. Technology can help, but it also reveals new obstacles. Smartphones and keyboards are designed for large languages, so speakers of small ones often find that the letters or accents they need are missing and give up writing messages in their own tongue. Volunteers have therefore designed new keyboards and free apps that teach vocabulary through games. Perhaps more important, teenagers in several communities now share jokes and music videos online in the minority language, showing that it can sound modern and fun rather than old-fashioned.

E. A few languages have been revived after losing their last native speakers, usually by learning from old texts and recordings. Revivals face an unusual problem: a language that stopped being used decades ago has no words for mobile phones or climate change. Committees must invent them, often by combining old roots or borrowing from relatives of the language, and disputes are common. Purists want new vocabulary to follow traditional patterns, whereas pragmatists prefer whatever younger speakers will actually accept and use.

F. How should success be measured? Counting speakers is misleading if they are all elderly, so many experts focus on whether children learn the language from their parents, which they regard as the decisive sign of health. Practical support matters too. Laws granting a language official status oblige public bodies to offer services in it, and employers who use it in the workplace give young people a reason to keep it. Yet funding for such measures is often short-term, depending on the priorities of whichever government is in power.

title: Charting the Hidden Seabed
context:
A. Humans have produced more detailed maps of the surface of Mars than of their own planet's ocean floor. Only about a quarter of the seabed has been charted in high resolution, and the rest is known from rough estimates. The main reason is physical. Light fades within a few hundred metres of the surface, and radio waves and radar, which allow satellites to survey land in fine detail, are absorbed almost immediately by seawater. Anyone wishing to see the bottom of the sea must therefore rely on sound.

B. For centuries, the only way to measure depth was the lead line: a sailor lowered a weighted rope until it touched the bottom and then hauled it back to read the length. In deep water a single measurement could take several hours, and ships might sail for weeks and record only a handful of figures. Real progress came in the nineteenth century, when companies wished to lay telegraph cables between continents and needed to know whether the route crossed cliffs or gentle plains.

C. Modern ships use echo sounders, which send a pulse of sound downwards and calculate depth from the time the echo takes to return. Multibeam systems go further by emitting dozens or hundreds of narrow beams in a fan shape, so that a vessel maps a wide strip of seabed as it travels. The calculations are not simple, however. Sound moves faster in warm, salty water than in cold, fresh water, so crews must measure the temperature and salinity of the sea at different depths and correct their figures accordingly.

D. Satellites cannot see the bottom directly, but they can detect its influence. A large undersea mountain has enough mass to attract water towards it by gravity, producing a slight bulge on the surface that radar altimeters can measure from orbit. Converting these bulges into maps gives only coarse detail, with features smaller than a few kilometres lost, yet the method has revealed thousands of previously unknown seamounts. It is also cheap compared with ship surveys, because a single satellite covers the entire globe repeatedly.

E. Robotic submarines are now being used to fill the gaps. Programmed in advance, they travel for days without a crew and fly only a few dozen metres above the seabed, producing images far sharper than any ship can achieve from the surface. Their weakness is energy: batteries limit how far they can go before they must be recovered. Another strategy is to ask ordinary vessels, from fishing boats to private yachts, to share the depth readings their instruments already collect, building a map from thousands of small contributions.

F. An international project aims to complete a map of the entire ocean floor by 2030. Detailed charts would improve computer models of tsunamis, which depend on how waves are shaped by underwater terrain, and would help scientists to locate the ridges and canyons where fish are most abundant. Some conservationists, however, fear that better maps will also guide companies towards minerals on the seabed, opening the way to mining whose effects on deep-sea life are poorly understood.

title: Farming in Towers
context:
A. In a vertical farm, crops are grown in layers stacked from floor to ceiling inside a warehouse or purpose-built tower, rather than across open fields. Plants receive light from LED lamps tuned to the wavelengths they use most efficiently, and their roots hang in nutrient-rich water or mist instead of soil. Because every layer is a growing surface, one hectare of floor space can produce as much as several dozen hectares of conventional farmland, according to the industry's own estimates, which independent researchers regard as optimistic but plausible for certain crops.

B. Supporters emphasise the saving of natural resources. The water that plants do not absorb is collected, cleaned and reused, so these farms can use up to ninety-five per cent less water than field agriculture. Since the growing rooms are sealed, insects are kept out and chemical pesticides are rarely needed. Fertiliser also stays inside the system instead of draining into rivers, where it normally feeds algae and harms fish. For regions facing water shortages, these features make the technology particularly attractive.

C. The weak point is electricity. Lamps must replace the sun for up to eighteen hours a day, and lighting alone typically accounts for the largest share of operating costs. Several well-funded start-ups have closed after energy prices rose faster than they had forecast. Surviving companies try to reduce the problem by buying wind or solar power under long contracts, by using more efficient lamps and by locating farms in places with cheap night-time electricity.

D. Not every crop suits the model. Lettuce, spinach, basil and other leafy plants grow fast, stay small and sell at a good price per kilogram, so they dominate production. Strawberries and tomatoes have also been grown successfully. Staple grains such as wheat and rice, in contrast, need far more space and sunlight per tonne and sell for so little that no indoor system can compete. Vertical farms are therefore unlikely to feed the world's basic calorie needs, whatever their enthusiasts claim.

E. Location is a further advantage. A farm can be built inside or beside a city, so that produce travels a few kilometres rather than hundreds, arriving fresher and with less spoilage on the way. The approach also allows people to grow salad crops in places where it would otherwise be impossible, such as deserts or regions with long, freezing winters. Because the interior climate is controlled, harvests are not threatened by floods, droughts or sudden frosts, which makes supply easier to plan.

F. Running a vertical farm resembles operating a factory more than tending a field. Sensors track temperature, humidity and the nutrient content of the water, and software adjusts them continuously to speed up growth. Such systems need technicians and data analysts rather than traditional farm labourers. Critics also raise less technical doubts: some chefs say that indoor produce lacks the flavour of sun-grown plants, and surveys show that a share of shoppers distrust food grown without soil or natural light.

title: A Short History of Spectacles
context:
A. Long before spectacles existed, scholars struggled with ageing eyesight. Around the eleventh century, monks who copied manuscripts began to use reading stones, polished domes of quartz or clear glass laid directly on the page to magnify the letters. The stone was held or slid along the line, which made reading slow, but it allowed people with weakening vision to continue the work that gave them their livelihood. These devices survive today mainly in monastery museums.

B. Wearable glasses appeared in northern Italy in the late thirteenth century. They consisted of two convex lenses, each set in a frame of wood, bone or metal and joined by a rivet, and they were pinched onto the nose. No one knows who made the first pair, because early records are silent and later writers invented stories to fill the gap. What is certain is that craftsmen in Venice treated the new product seriously: the city's glassmakers' guild issued rules about how lenses should be made and punished those who sold poor imitations.

C. Demand grew steadily, then sharply. When the printing press spread across Europe in the fifteenth century, books became affordable to ordinary families, and many readers discovered that they needed help with small print. Early lenses, though, only corrected far-sighted vision. Glasses for short-sighted people, using concave lenses, did not become common until roughly a century later. As workshops multiplied and techniques improved, the price of a pair fell, bringing spectacles within reach of tradesmen as well as scholars and nobles.

D. For centuries the frame was the weakest part. Early designs rested on the nose alone and slipped constantly, so wearers invented solutions such as spectacles on a stick held in the hand, or lenses clipped to the nose, known as pince-nez. Only in the eighteenth century did an optician in London popularise side arms, called temples, that rest on the ears. Even then, glasses carried a stigma in some societies, because wearing them could signal old age or physical weakness, and fashionable people often carried them but rarely put them on.

E. Scientific understanding transformed lens-making in the nineteenth century. Doctors learned that blurred vision usually results from the shape of the eyeball, which led to proper tests with standard charts of letters of decreasing size. An astronomer in the 1820s ground a cylindrical lens to correct his own distorted vision, an early treatment of what is now called astigmatism. Meanwhile, bifocals, which combine two focal zones in one lens, are traditionally credited to the American statesman Benjamin Franklin, who disliked changing between two pairs.

F. Modern materials have made glasses lighter and tougher. Plastic has largely replaced glass in lenses, and thin metal alloys have replaced heavy frames. Contact lenses, which sit directly on the surface of the eye, offer a frame-free alternative, and laser surgery can permanently reshape the cornea. Yet the problem is far from solved. Public health researchers estimate that hundreds of millions of people still lack the glasses they need, mostly in poorer regions where eye tests are unavailable, which limits their ability to learn and to work.

title: When Cities Run Hot
context:
A. On a calm summer night, the centre of a large city can be three to five degrees warmer than the countryside only a few kilometres away. This effect, known as the urban heat island, was first described by a London chemist in the early nineteenth century, who compared thermometer readings taken in the capital with those from fields outside. Dark materials such as asphalt and roof tiles absorb sunshine all day and release the stored heat slowly after sunset, so the difference is greatest in the hours before dawn.

B. Several factors combine to create the effect. Vegetation cools the air by releasing water vapour, and cities have far less of it than rural areas. Cars, factories and above all air-conditioning units give off heat as a by-product, adding to the load. Tall buildings packed closely together form what planners call street canyons, which obstruct the wind that might otherwise carry warm air away. In a dense district, each of these influences strengthens the others.

C. The consequences go beyond discomfort. During heatwaves, deaths rise sharply among elderly residents, who often live alone and may not realise how dangerous high indoor temperatures are. Mapping studies in many countries show that poorer neighbourhoods tend to have fewer trees and more pavement, so the people with least money to spend on cooling are exposed to the most heat. Demand for electricity also jumps when everyone switches on air conditioning at once, and in some cities this has led to power cuts at the worst possible moment.

D. Planting is the most natural remedy. Measurements show that the air beneath the canopy of a mature tree can be several degrees cooler than that on an open street, because leaves both shade the ground and release moisture. Where space on the ground is scarce, builders are turning to roofs and walls, covering them with soil and plants. Ponds, fountains and restored streams offer a further benefit, as evaporating water draws heat from the surrounding air, although such features are costly to maintain.

E. An alternative is to change the colour of the city. White or pale roofs reflect most sunlight instead of absorbing it, and light-coloured paving does the same. One large American city has painted entire streets with a reflective coating, lowering their surface temperature noticeably. Such measures reduce the need for air conditioning inside buildings. They have drawbacks, however: reflective surfaces can create glare for pedestrians, and in cold climates they give up the free warmth that dark roofs capture during winter.

F. Cities that take the problem seriously begin by measuring it. Thermal cameras on satellites reveal the hottest districts, allowing money for new trees to be spent where it will help most. Planners are also reconsidering layout, leaving corridors between tall buildings aligned with prevailing winds so that breezes can reach the centre. Some local authorities have introduced building regulations that require new roofs to meet a minimum standard of reflectivity. With global temperatures rising, experts expect the pressure for such rules to grow rather than fade.

title: Tiny Plastics in Rivers and Lakes
context:
A. Microplastics are pieces of plastic smaller than five millimetres across. Scientists divide them into two groups. Primary microplastics are manufactured at that size, such as the tiny beads once added to face scrubs and toothpaste, or the pellets that factories melt to make larger products. Secondary microplastics form when bigger objects, from bottles to fishing nets, are broken down by sunlight, waves and friction. Because the second group arises from litter already in the environment, it is the more difficult to prevent.

B. A major route into rivers is the household washing machine. Clothes made of polyester or nylon shed tiny threads, and one load of laundry may release hundreds of thousands of them into the drain. Another large source is the wear of vehicle tyres on roads, which produces fine rubber-and-plastic dust that rain washes into streams. Paints, ropes and artificial turf add smaller contributions. Together these sources mean that microplastics reach freshwater even in areas where people take care not to drop litter.

C. Counting microplastics in a lake is laborious. Researchers tow a net with very fine mesh behind a boat, filter the catch and then examine it under a microscope. Suspect fragments are tested with infrared light, because each type of plastic absorbs a different pattern of wavelengths, which allows the polymer to be identified. A recurring frustration is that teams use different mesh sizes and counting rules, so results from one study often cannot be compared with those of another.

D. Laboratory experiments show that small animals at the base of the food chain, such as water fleas, readily swallow plastic particles and may eat less real food as a result. Microplastics can also act like sponges: chemical pollutants and bacteria stick to their surfaces and may be carried into living tissue. However, some scientists point out that many experiments use concentrations far higher than those found in nature, so the harm seen in the laboratory may overstate what happens in rivers.

E. Traces of plastic have been found in tap water and bottled water, and in everyday foods including salt. Whether the quantities pose a risk to human health is still unknown. Sewage plants capture the great majority of particles, often over ninety per cent, but the volume of water they treat is so large that enormous numbers still escape. Moreover, the solid sludge left over is frequently spread on farmland as fertiliser, which can transfer plastic from the sewer to the soil and eventually back into streams.

F. Responses are emerging at several levels. A number of countries have banned microbeads in cosmetics, and inventors are developing filters that can be fitted to washing machines to catch fibres before they leave the house. Tyre manufacturers are experimenting with compounds that shed less dust. Volunteer groups also play a part, collecting water samples from local streams and sending them to universities, which gives researchers far more data than their own budgets would allow.

title: Can We Trust Eyewitnesses?
context:
A. Most people imagine that memory works like a video camera, storing events exactly as they happened and replaying them on request. Psychologists have shown that this picture is wrong. Remembering is an act of reconstruction: each time we recall an event, the brain rebuilds it from fragments and fills the gaps with what seems likely. These additions feel exactly like genuine memories, and the person recalling them cannot tell which parts are real, which is why honest witnesses can be sincerely mistaken.

B. A well-known series of experiments in the 1970s showed how easily recollections can be altered. Volunteers watched short films of traffic collisions and were then asked to estimate the speed of the cars. Those who were asked how fast the cars had 'smashed' into each other gave higher estimates than those who were asked about cars that had 'hit' each other. A week later, the first group were also more likely to say they had seen broken glass, although none appeared in the film.

C. Emotion affects what the mind records. In a violent crime, a witness's attention often fixes on a weapon, leaving little capacity to notice the attacker's face, a phenomenon known as weapon focus. Very high stress can further impair the formation of detailed memories. Surprisingly, the confidence with which a witness speaks is a poor guide to accuracy: studies repeatedly find that people who are certain are wrong almost as often as those who hesitate, yet juries tend to believe the confident.

D. Police often ask witnesses to pick a suspect from a set of photographs or a row of people. Experiments show that if the real culprit is absent, many witnesses choose the person who looks most similar to him instead of saying that nobody matches. To reduce this error, some forces use a double-blind procedure in which the officer running the line-up does not know which person is the suspect, so that he cannot guide the witness by accident. Showing the faces one at a time rather than together also helps.

E. Memory is fragile over time. Much detail is lost in the first hours, and what remains can be altered when witnesses talk to one another, because each person absorbs elements of the others' accounts without noticing. News coverage can have the same effect. For this reason, investigators try to interview witnesses separately and soon after the event, using open invitations such as 'tell me everything you remember' rather than leading questions that suggest an answer.

F. The legal consequences are serious. In the United States, DNA testing has overturned hundreds of convictions, and analysis of those cases shows that mistaken eyewitness identification played a part in the large majority. In response, many courts now give juries a warning that confident testimony is not necessarily accurate, and judges may allow psychologists to explain the research as expert witnesses. Even so, trial lawyers admit that a witness who points at the defendant and says 'it was him' is still extremely persuasive.
